road/pair: Take a two pixel image, x zero, as a point in the plane, and some noise, epsilon, as another.
road/arc: The diffusion blend joins them: as alpha bar falls, it slides from the image to the noise, and in this plane its path is a curve.
road/back: To make a new image, walk that path backwards: from the noise toward the image, each step the way the path points where you stand.
road/drift: On a curve, big steps go wrong: each heads off straight while the path bends away, and two of them end far from the image.
road/many: Small steps hug the curve, but then the walk takes many of them.
road/straight: A straight path has no bend to fall off. One step, the way it points, lands exactly on the image.
road/liu: That is the idea of rectified flow, from Shing-chow Liu and colleagues in 2022: rectified means made straight, since a straight path can be followed exactly.
road/lipman: A month later, Yaron Lipman and colleagues reached straight paths too, and named the method: flow matching.
line/line: Flow matching uses the straight line. Its point at time t, x t, is one minus t, times x zero, plus t times epsilon.
line/t: Here t runs from zero, the image, to one, pure noise.
line/point: At t of a quarter, take three quarters of x zero, plus a quarter of epsilon: a half, and a half.
line/v: As t grows, the point slides along at a steady pace. How far it moves per unit of t is its velocity, v. Over the whole line it travels from the image to the noise, so v is epsilon minus x zero.
line/steady: Here that is minus two and two, at every t. On the curve, the direction kept turning; on the line, it never does.
train/net: Train the network as for diffusion, with a new target. It sees x t and t, and guesses the velocity: v hat, the hat marking a guess.
train/loss: The loss is the squared error against epsilon minus x zero, averaged. A guess of minus one and a half, and two, misses by a half and by zero: the loss is a quarter over two, zero point one two five.
train/cross: Train on many images, each with its own noise, and their lines criss-cross. These two pass the same point at the same t, with different velocities.
train/average: The network sees only the point and t, not the line, so its best guess is their average: that is where the squared error is smallest.
train/flow: Arrows at every point, carrying points along like water in a stream, are called a flow. Training matches the network's flow to the lines: flow matching.
sample/start: To make an image, start at t of one, with fresh noise, and walk back to zero.
sample/dt: Pick a step size, delta t: the change in t per step. With delta t of a half, two steps get from one to zero.
sample/rule: Each step asks the network for v hat where the point is, and moves against it, back toward the image: the new x t is the old one, minus delta t times v hat.
sample/ex: Start from minus one and two, with a guess of minus two and two. Half the guess is minus one and one; take that away, and the point lands on zero and one, at t of a half.
sample/exact: A second step lands on one and zero: the image. With a velocity that never changes, one step of delta t equal to one would land there too.
sample/euler: Stepping the way an arrow points, then looking again, is Oiler's method, from Leonhard Oiler in 1768. Gradient descent steps the same way: w gets w minus eta g.
sample/bend: The network's arrows are averages, though, so its paths bend, and samplers take a few steps rather than one.
